title: Visual perception of materials and their properties
research_question: How does the visual system perceive materials and their properties, and what theoretical framework best explains this, particularly through 'statistical appearance models'?

participants.description: Not applicable; this is a theoretical review synthesizing findings from various empirical studies with human observers.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Photographs of real materials (e.g., fruit, wax simulacra, textiles, stones, liquids, foodstuffs).

Computer-simulated renderings of various materials (e.g., glossy spheres, stucco reliefs, transparent filters, crumpled sheets) under different illumination conditions, shapes, and surface properties.
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and various sections describing cited experiments

measures.instrument: Identification tasks (e.g., identifying materials from photographs, distinguishing real vs. fake materials)
Subjective ratings (e.g., hardness, glossiness, prettiness, roughness, translucency, refractive index, hue)
Matching tasks (e.g., adjusting reflectance parameters of one sphere to match another, matching refractive index)
Subjective ratings (e.g., size, contrast, distinctness of highlights)

findings.consequent: Ability to recognize and categorize materials
findings.mechanism: Visual system uses characteristic image features for rapid identification.
findings.quote: human observers are good at recognizing and categorizing materials.

findings.antecedent: Visual presentation of materials from different categories
findings.consequent: Ability to classify materials through visual judgments of their properties (e.g., hardness, glossiness, prettiness)
findings.mechanism: Subjective ratings of individual samples systematically cluster into categories.
findings.quote: subjective ratings of the individual samples were systematically clustered into categories

findings.antecedent: Brief visual presentation (40 ms) of real vs. fake materials
findings.consequent: Ability to distinguish between real and fake materials and describe properties
findings.mechanism: Subjects rapidly identify subtle appearance differences ('look') of materials.
findings.quote: subjects were able to make remarkably precise descriptions of the properties of materials and were above chance performance

findings.antecedent: Computer-simulated glossy surfaces under natural illumination
findings.mechanism: Visual system uses statistical structure of illumination typical of natural environments.
findings.quote: this ability generalizes across differences in lighting, as long as the illumination has statistical structure that is typical of the natural environment.

findings.mechanism: Perceived glossiness is systematically affected by low-level image properties related to illumination statistics.
findings.quote: varying the statistical characteristics of the illumination has systematic effects on perceived glossiness

findings.mechanism: Multisensory cues contribute to the perception of specular reflectance.
findings.quote: Judgments of specular reflectance are affected by both binocular disparity and motion information

findings.antecedent: Properties of highlights (brightness, position, orientation relative to diffuse shading)
findings.mechanism: Highlights are defining visual characteristics of glossy surfaces, and their properties serve as cues.
findings.quote: properties of highlights, including their brightness, position and orientation relative to diffuse shading on the surface

findings.antecedent: Skewness of luminance histograms of stucco reliefs
findings.mechanism: Visual system uses image statistics like skewness to distinguish glossy from matte surfaces.
findings.quote: increasing the skewness of images of matte stucco reliefs made the surfaces appear glossy.

findings.mechanism: Simple image statistics like skewness are not sufficient to predict perceived glossiness.
findings.quote: skewness is neither necessary nor sufficient to predict perceived glossiness

findings.mechanism: Illumination geometry biases judgments of surface roughness.
findings.quote: glancing illumination angles make surfaces appear rougher than frontal illumination.

findings.consequent: Visual system's ability to separate single image intensity values into multiple causal layers ('scission')
findings.mechanism: Specific image structures enable the visual system to decompose image information into causal layers.
findings.quote: photometric and geometric conditions that cause the visual system to separate single image intensity values into multiple causal layers

findings.antecedent: Solid transparent and translucent objects (e.g., ice-cube, wax candle)
findings.mechanism: These materials behave differently from thin filters, appearing to transmit light even when typical 'scission' conditions are not met.
findings.quote: solid transparent and translucent objects... behave quite differently from thin transparent filters, and appear subjectively to transmit light even when these photometric and geometric image conditions are not met

findings.antecedent: Shadow regions and relationships between shading and highlights
findings.mechanism: Shadows and shading-highlight relationships provide information about sub-surface scattering.
moderators_reported: contrast and blur of non-specular components
findings.quote: shadow regions are likely to play a role... relationships between shading and highlights provide important information about whether an object is translucent.

findings.antecedent: Thickness of transparent object and distance to background
findings.consequent: Judgments of refractive index of solid transparent materials
findings.mechanism: Judgments are biased by scene variables that affect image distortion, even if irrelevant to intrinsic material properties.
findings.quote: judgments were substantially biased by the thickness of the object and the distance to the background.

findings.antecedent: Illumination conditions (natural vs. unnatural noise environment)
findings.mechanism: Gloss perception relies on characteristic signatures of specular reflection; when environmental statistics are infringed, perception breaks down.
findings.quote: when the spheres were illuminated under unnatural illuminations... performance decreased significantly.

findings.mechanism: Complex, non-monotonic interactions between scene variables affect highlight appearance, leading to 'contamination' between judgments.
findings.quote: when asked to estimate the glossiness of the surface, the judgments varied significantly depending on the depth of the relief.

findings.antecedent: Low-level image properties of highlights (size, contrast, distinctness)
findings.mechanism: Subjects use highlight salience as a 'proxy' for estimating intrinsic physical surface parameters, reflecting how variations in material properties manifest in the image.
findings.quote: a simple weighted combination of these latter judgments accounted for all the main trends in the glossiness judgments

findings.antecedent: Thickness of transparent object and distance to background
findings.mechanism: Visual system uses image distortion as a cue for refractive materials; judgments are biased by scene variables affecting distortion.
findings.quote: subjects' matches were substantially biased by the thickness or distance of the object, even though these scene variables have nothing to do with the intrinsic properties of the material.

findings.mechanism: Hue is a circular dimension in subjective appearance, which does not directly map to the linear physical dimension of wavelength, suggesting the visual system does not primarily estimate physical spectra.

mechanisms: Statistical generative models: The brain builds internal models that capture natural degrees of variation in appearance between material samples, rather than estimating physical parameters. These models identify statistically informative appearance attributes (e.g., highlight size, contrast) that vary parametrically between samples.

Image statistics approach: The visual system relies on characteristic statistical 'signatures' in the image that reliably correlate with material properties across varying viewing conditions, without explicitly estimating and discounting illumination/geometry.

Inverse optics: The visual system explicitly estimates and 'discounts' the contributions of illumination and geometry to observed intensity values to reconstruct physical properties of the scene (e.g., light sources, surface geometry, reflectance parameters).

Perceptual organization mechanisms: General-purpose mechanisms parse the image into salient regions or features (e.g., highlights, shadows) to form initial hypotheses about how appearance features might vary.

Mid-level visual processes: These processes detect consistency in image-level features (e.g., directions of intensity gradients attributed to different causes) to express photo-geometric constraints, rather than requiring explicit world coordinate estimates.
moderators: Contrast and blur of non-specular components
limitations: The visual system is far from perfect, exhibiting 'partial' constancy and mis-estimates of surface reflectance properties.
The visual system can be fooled when the assumed statistics of the world are infringed (e.g., by unnatural illumination).
There is a 'chicken and egg' problem in inverse optics: estimating lighting requires knowing reflectance, and vice versa.
It is unclear how perceptual organization mechanisms (e.g., 'scission') work, how the visual system learns initial hypotheses, or how new evidence is incorporated into appearance models.
It is unclear how different senses (e.g., vision, haptics) are compared and combined to yield a multi-sensory impression of material properties.
It is unclear to what extent semantic knowledge about materials influences perceptual processing.
It is unclear what limits the ability to generalize perceptual knowledge about specific materials or classes to novel viewing situations.
